original_question: Does there exist a universal countable right-orderable group?
target_in_paper: Section 2.1, Problem 2.19: "Is there a universal countable right-orderable group?"
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's official formulation essentially verbatim: it has the correct class of groups (right-orderable groups), the correct size restriction (countable), and the correct universality question. It also stays narrowly focused on the exact open problem rather than drifting to nearby questions about right-ordered, locally indicable, finitely generated, or finitely presented groups.
missing_details: The phrase "universal" should be made explicit: universal for the class of countable right-orderable groups, meaning that every countable right-orderable group embeds into the proposed group as a subgroup (equivalently, as an abstract group embedding).
The phrase "right-orderable" should be defined stand-alone: a group is right-orderable if it admits a total order preserved by right multiplication.

To stay paper-faithful, the question should not be silently replaced by the adjacent but different right-ordered version, where the embedding is order-preserving and the paper gives a negative argument in the comments.
It helps to specify that the sought universal object itself is countable and right-orderable.
refined_question: Does there exist a countable right-orderable group U such that every countable right-orderable group G embeds into U as a group, where "right-orderable" means that G admits a total order invariant under right multiplication?
justification: The draft is targeting exactly Section 2.1, Problem 2.19 (p. 10), whose wording is the same as your draft. The only refinements needed are to unpack the implicit meanings of "universal" and "right-orderable" so that the question is self-contained. The introductory paragraph of Section 2 explains the ambient notion of a right ordering as a total order preserved by multiplication on the right (Section 2, introductory text, p. 9). The comment on Problem 2.19 shows why this unpacking matters: the paper distinguishes the open right-orderable problem from the different right-ordered problem, noting that there is no universal countable right-ordered group by the given argument, while Problem 2.19 itself remains open (Section 2.3, comment on 2.19, p. 14). So the refined question should keep the exact right-orderable scope and make subgroup-universality explicit, but should not broaden or alter the target problem.
